chapter.name: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification

questions.q: Narsimha, a farmer near Warangal, keeps seed of three paddy varieties: one tolerates drought, one resists a common pest and one grows well in poor soil. A dry year arrives with a pest outbreak. Why is his risk of losing the whole crop lower than that of a neighbour who sows one variety?
questions.a: At least one of his varieties is likely to cope with each stress, so the whole crop does not fail together. The chapter says diversity reduces the risk of crop failure because varieties carry different useful characteristics (drought tolerance, pest resistance, growth in nutrient-poor soil).
o: At least one of his varieties is likely to cope with each stress, so the whole crop does not fail together
Growing three varieties together makes every one of them drought tolerant and pest resistant
Pests avoid any field in which more than one variety is sown, so no variety is ever attacked
Mixed sowing turns poor soil into fertile soil within one season

questions.q: A forest block holds 45 endemic species but is almost untouched, with its original forest cover intact. Using the chapter's definition, how should it be described?
questions.a: Rich in endemic species but not a hotspot yet, because a hotspot also needs significant habitat loss. A biodiversity hotspot has two conditions: a large number of endemic species AND significant habitat loss.
o: Rich in endemic species but not a hotspot yet, because a hotspot also needs significant habitat loss
A biodiversity hotspot, because a large number of endemic species is enough on its own
Not important for conservation, because no habitat has been lost
A hotspot only if it lies in mountains in the north of India

questions.q: A Lion-tailed macaque born in a zoo in another country is shown to a class. A student says, 'So this species is not endemic to India.' What is the best reply?
questions.a: The species is still endemic to India, because endemic refers to where it occurs naturally and nowhere else. Endemic species are restricted to a particular region and not found naturally anywhere else; a captive animal elsewhere does not change where the species occurs naturally.
o: The species is still endemic to India, because endemic refers to where it occurs naturally and nowhere else
The student is right, because even a single captive animal abroad is enough to cancel its endemism
The species is endemic only to the zoo where it was born
Endemic means the species is found in every region of the world

questions.q: After heavy pollution, the microscopic algae of a coastal sea sharply decline. Which function listed in the chapter would be affected most directly?
questions.a: The release of oxygen into the water and air. The chapter assigns the release of most of our oxygen to microscopic ocean algae; pollination, decomposition and food-making by land plants are done by other groups.
o: The release of oxygen into the water and air
The pollination of flowers by bats and bees
The conversion of fallen leaves into manure
The capture of sunlight by tall forest trees

questions.q:
Statement 1: Microscopic algae in the oceans release most of the oxygen we breathe.
Statement 2: Any region that has many endemic species is, for that reason alone, a biodiversity hotspot.
Statement 3: The diversity of life seen today is the outcome of small differences among individuals that affected survival and reproduction and accumulated over many generations.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only. Statement 2 is false, because a hotspot also needs significant habitat loss; statements 1 and 3 match the chapter.
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 3 only
Statement 2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Farmers who conserve several crop varieties lower the risk of crop failure.
Reason (R): The varieties differ in useful traits such as drought tolerance, pest resistance and growth in nutrient-poor soil.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The differing traits are exactly why a single stress rarely destroys every variety at once, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A region becomes a biodiversity hotspot only when it has many endemic species and has also suffered significant ___.
questions.a: habitat loss

questions.q:
Match each item in List I with the matching item in List II.
1. Nilgiri tahr
2. Western Ghats
3. Microscopic algae of the oceans
4. Fungi and bacteria on the forest floor
a. Release most of the oxygen we breathe
b. An endemic species of India
c. Turn fallen leaves and waste into manure
d. A global biodiversity hotspot
questions.a: 1-b, 2-d, 3-a, 4-c. Nilgiri tahr is an endemic species; the Western Ghats is a hotspot; ocean algae release oxygen; fungi and bacteria decompose leaves into manure.

questions.q: True or False? Every biodiversity hotspot has a large number of endemic species, but a region with many endemic species is not necessarily a hotspot. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. A hotspot needs both many endemic species and significant habitat loss, so the second condition can be missing in a region rich in endemic species.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: a hotspot needs many endemic species AND significant habitat loss, so endemic richness alone is not enough

questions.q:
India has mountains in the north, desert in the west, rainforests in the North East, plateaus in the south and long coastlines.
(a) Name two of these habitats that the chapter says support a wide variety of species.
(b) State what differs from region to region that helps explain this variety.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: mountains, desert, rainforest, plateau, coastline. (b) Each region has different soil types and different climatic conditions such as temperature and rainfall.
s: Part (a): any two of mountains, desert, rainforest, plateau, coastline
Part (b): distinct soil types and climatic conditions (temperature, rainfall)

questions.q:
A cotton cooperative in Adilabad plans to sow a single variety on all its land.
(a) Which risk does the chapter say rises when a farmer relies on one variety?
(b) What did farmers do for centuries to lower that risk?
questions.a: (a) The risk of crop failure. (b) They conserved diverse crop varieties with useful traits such as drought tolerance, pest resistance and growth in nutrient-poor soils.
s: Part (a): crop failure (weaker food security)
Part (b): conserved diverse varieties with useful characteristics

questions.q: Distinguish between an endemic species and a biodiversity hotspot. Give one example of each from India.
questions.a: An endemic species is found naturally only in one region and nowhere else (e.g. Nilgiri tahr). A hotspot is a region with many endemic species that has suffered significant habitat loss (e.g. Western Ghats).
s: Endemic species: found naturally only in one region, with an example
Hotspot: many endemic species plus significant habitat loss, with an example

questions.q: Explain in two points why the biodiversity seen on Earth today is called an outcome of continuous change.
questions.a: Small differences among individuals affected their chances of survival and reproduction as conditions changed; these differences accumulated over many generations and gave rise to new forms of life.
s: Small differences affected survival and reproduction under changed conditions
The differences accumulated over many generations into new forms of life

questions.q: Rohan says, 'Biodiversity just means the number of animal species in a forest, and it matters only to scientists.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. Biodiversity is the variety of all living organisms, including microorganisms and plants, and everyone depends on it for oxygen, manure, pollination, food, shelter, medicines and livelihoods.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Biodiversity covers all living organisms, not only animals
Humans depend on it for food, shelter, medicines and livelihoods

questions.q: Describe an imaginary region that qualifies as a biodiversity hotspot. State the two conditions it meets and name one real hotspot of India.
questions.a: E.g. a hill region with 80 species found nowhere else whose forest has been cleared over a large part of its area meets both conditions (many endemic species, significant habitat loss). Real examples: Western Ghats or Indo-Burma.
s: A described region with many endemic species
The same region has suffered significant habitat loss
A correct real hotspot of India named

questions.q: Sangam Tinai and sacred groves are mentioned in the chapter. Explain how these customs protected nature although they were not stated as a formal ecological theory.
questions.a: Sangam Tinai classified landscapes, showing a deep understanding of landscapes and their living things; sacred groves were protected by custom, so locally diverse habitats were preserved in line with present ecological principles.
s: Sangam Tinai classified landscapes and showed understanding of their living things
Sacred groves were protected by custom
Result: locally diverse habitats were preserved, matching ecological principles

questions.q:
Four fields of 2.5 hectares each give 30 quintals of paddy in a normal year. Field A carries a drought-tolerant variety, B a pest-resistant variety, C a variety for poor soil and D a high-yield variety that fails completely in drought. In a drought year A loses 10%, B loses 60%, C loses 60% and D loses all. A neighbour sows only variety D on four such fields.
(i) Find the normal total harvest.
(ii) Find the total harvest of the farmer in the drought year.
(iii) Find the neighbour's harvest in the drought year.
(iv) Name the trait that saved most of the farmer's harvest.
(v) State what this shows about diversity and food security.
questions.a: (i) 120 quintals (ii) 27 + 12 + 12 + 0 = 51 quintals (iii) 0 quintals (iv) drought tolerance of variety A (v) A mix of varieties lowers the risk of crop failure and strengthens food security.
s: Normal total 4 x 30 = 120 quintals
Drought year 27 + 12 + 12 + 0 = 51 quintals
Neighbour: all four fields fail, 0 quintals
Drought tolerance (variety A) saved most of the harvest
Diversity spreads risk and strengthens food security

questions.q:
A survey compares three forest regions. Region X: 120 endemic species, 70% of its original 10,000 sq km forest cleared. Region Y: 150 endemic species, forest almost untouched. Region Z: 10 endemic species, 60% of its forest cleared.
(i) Which region is a biodiversity hotspot by the chapter's definition?
(ii) How many sq km of forest remain in X?
(iii) Give the reason Y is not a hotspot.
(iv) Give the reason Z is not a hotspot.
(v) With funds for only one region, which should receive them first? Justify.
questions.a: (i) X (ii) 3000 sq km (iii) Y has many endemic species but no significant habitat loss (iv) Z has habitat loss but few endemic species (v) X first, because it has both many endemic species and heavy loss, so action there saves the most species at risk.
s: X is the hotspot
10,000 x 30% = 3,000 sq km remain
Y lacks significant habitat loss
Z lacks a large number of endemic species
Justified choice of X using both conditions (a reasoned case for Y as safe-for-now is also accepted)

questions.q:
Harini surveys 250 plant species along a stretch of the Western Ghats. Of these, 60 grow naturally nowhere else. She also learns that about a third of the original forest cover has been cleared for plantations. During the survey she sees a Lion-tailed macaque.
(a) What percentage of the plant species are endemic?
(b) Does her data meet both conditions for a biodiversity hotspot? Explain.
(c) Why is the macaque sighting more important for conservation than the sighting of a species found across all of India?
(d) A plantation company asks to clear 50 more hectares for jobs. Give one point for and one against, and state your decision.
questions.a: (a) 24% (b) Yes: 24% endemic is a large number and a third of the forest is lost (c) the macaque is endemic, so if its habitat goes it is lost from the world (d) a reasoned decision weighing jobs against loss of endemic habitat
s: Both conditions: many endemic species and significant habitat loss
Endemic species exist nowhere else, so its habitat loss is a global loss
A reasoned decision with one point on each side

questions.q:
Village P sows a single paddy variety on 200 acres, yielding 25 quintals per acre. Village Q sows four varieties on 50 acres each, averaging 20 quintals per acre. In a bad pest year a pest destroys 80% of one variety, the one that is the only variety in P and one of the four in Q.
(a) Find the normal harvest of each village.
(b) Find each village's harvest in the pest year.
(c) Which of the traits named in the chapter would protect the varieties in Q?
(d) The block office offers P-type seed free of cost. If pest years occur once in every three years, which village does better over time? Justify.
questions.a: (a) P 5000 q, Q 4000 q (b) P 1000 q, Q 3200 q (c) pest resistance, drought tolerance, growth in poor soil (d) Q does better when pest years exceed about 31% of years, since 1 in 3 is about 33%
s: Traits: pest resistance, drought tolerance, growth in nutrient-poor soil
Break-even p = 1000/3200 = 0.3125; one in three years is above it, so mixed Q does better

questions.q: A zoo keeper makes one list of animals active by day and another of animals active by night. A visitor asks her to also make a list of meat-eaters and plant-eaters, and notices that the owl appears in the night list and in the meat-eaters list. What does this show?
questions.a: The same organism can fall into different groups depending on the criterion chosen. In Activity 12.1 the same organism fits different groups when the criterion changes; neither list is wrong.
o: The same organism can fall into different groups depending on the criterion chosen
The owl has been wrongly classified and must be removed from one list
Only one criterion is ever correct for grouping living organisms
Organisms active at night cannot be placed in any feeding group

questions.q: Under a microscope a scientist sees that a single-celled organism has no membrane-bound nucleus. Which classification criterion from the chapter has she used?
questions.a: Cell structure, whether the cell is eukaryotic or prokaryotic. Whether a cell is eukaryote or prokaryote is part of the 'cell structure' criterion; the other options describe different criteria.
o: Cell structure, whether the cell is eukaryotic or prokaryotic
Mode of nutrition, whether it is autotrophic or heterotrophic
Ecological role, whether it is a producer, consumer or decomposer
Reproduction, whether it multiplies by asexual or sexual means

questions.q: Four hornbill species live in the Pakke Tiger Reserve. They nest only in large, old trees with suitable cavities and feed on specific fruits. If the forest loses most of its large old trees, what is the most likely result?
questions.a: The hornbills would lose nesting sites and food, so their distribution in the forest would change or shrink. The Pakke case shows species distribution depends on tree size and fruit availability; losing old trees removes nesting sites and specific fruits.
o: The hornbills would lose nesting sites and food, so their distribution in the forest would change or shrink
The hornbills would simply shift to nesting on the forest floor
Only the species that eat the most fruit would be affected
Nothing, because birds do not depend on particular trees

questions.q: A botanist in Chennai and a botanist in Tokyo discuss the same newly found plant without any confusion about which plant they mean. Which benefit of biological classification does this best illustrate?
questions.a: It gives scientists all over the world a common system to discuss organisms. The sixth benefit listed is a common worldwide system; the other options are different benefits from the same list.
o: It gives scientists all over the world a common system to discuss organisms
It makes the study of organisms more organised and systematic
It helps identify organisms under threat of extinction
It shows how different organisms interact with one another

questions.q: Two organisms are found to have very similar DNA. What can the scientist most reasonably infer using the chapter's ideas?
questions.a: They are likely to share a common ancestry. Genetic similarity, studied through DNA, and similar features suggest that organisms have evolved from common ancestors.
o: They are likely to share a common ancestry
They must live in exactly the same habitat
They must have the same mode of nutrition
They must be the same size as adults

questions.q:
Statement 1: Biological classification is the system of grouping living organisms only according to their differences.
Statement 2: Genetic similarity, studied in detail using DNA, is one of the criteria used to classify organisms.
Statement 3: Similar features in organisms suggest that they have evolved from common ancestors.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only. Statement 1 is false because grouping uses similarities and/or differences; statements 2 and 3 match the chapter.
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements
Statement 1 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Biological classification helps scientists give names to newly discovered organisms.
Reason (R): Classification groups organisms only by their size.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. A is a listed benefit of classification, but R is false because many criteria such as nutrition, cell structure, ecological role and reproduction are used.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Pakke Tiger Reserve has recorded nearly 300 of India's about 1,300 bird species, which is about ___ percent of them.

A student records for a pond organism: it is made of one cell, its nucleus is bounded by a membrane, it has no cell wall and it makes its own food.
(a) Name the two criteria from the chapter's list that these observations fall under.
(b) What do similar features in two organisms suggest?
questions.a: (a) Cell structure (unicellular, nucleus type, no cell wall) and mode of nutrition (autotrophic). (b) They may have evolved from common ancestors.
s: Part (a): cell structure and mode of nutrition
Part (b): similar features suggest a common ancestry

questions.q:
In the chapter, an unsorted heap of thousands of books on a library floor is compared with the millions of organisms on Earth.
(a) What does the heap of books stand for in the analogy?
(b) What plays the part of sorting books into subjects and sections?
questions.a: (a) The millions of organisms with no system of grouping. (b) Biological classification.
s: Part (a): the huge number of ungrouped organisms
Part (b): biological classification

questions.q: Explain how classification helps conservation and how it helps scientists in different countries work together.
questions.a: It identifies organisms that are under threat of extinction so they can be protected, and it gives scientists everywhere a common system with which to discuss organisms.
s: Conservation: identifies organisms threatened with extinction
Communication: a common worldwide system of grouping and naming

questions.q: The four hornbills of Pakke are found in different parts of the forest. State the two needs of the birds that explain this, and say what this tells scientists.
questions.a: They nest only in large, old trees with cavities and feed on specific fruits, so the species occur where tree size and fruit availability suit them; this lets scientists ask precise questions about how species are distributed and linked to plants.
s: Needs: large old nesting trees with cavities and specific fruits
Inference: distribution depends on tree size and fruit, so species can be studied precisely

questions.q: A mushroom grows on a dead log. Under which ecological role would it be grouped, and which classification criterion does that role belong to?
questions.a: It is a decomposer, because it feeds on dead organic matter; the criterion is ecological role (producer, consumer or decomposer).
s: Decomposer, feeding on dead organic matter
Criterion: ecological role

questions.q: Asha says, 'An eagle and a tiger can be put in one group by eating habits, but in different groups by external features, and both groupings are scientifically fine.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Yes. Grouping depends on the criterion chosen: both are carnivores (nutrition/eating habits) but their external features differ, so each criterion gives a valid but different grouping.
s: Verdict: the claim is correct
Same organisms group differently when the criterion changes
Example: carnivore by eating habits, separate by external features

questions.q: Write one row of your own for a grouping table like Table 12.2: choose a criterion, list three organisms that fit it, and state the feature that helped you decide.
questions.a: E.g. Criterion: ecological role as decomposer; organisms: mushroom, bread mould, bacteria that rot leaves; feature: they feed on dead organic matter.
s: A criterion from the chapter's list
Three organisms that really fit the criterion
The deciding feature stated

questions.q: Choose any three benefits of biological classification and match each with a situation in which a scientist would use it.
questions.a: E.g. organised study: sorting thousands of plants in a herbarium; identifying new organisms: comparing a new pond organism with known ones; conservation: spotting a species under threat of extinction.
s: Benefit 1 with a fitting situation
Benefit 2 with a fitting situation
Benefit 3 with a fitting situation

questions.q:
Five organisms are described. P: feathers, eats other animals. Q: feathers, eats fruits. R: thread-like, no chlorophyll, grows on dead logs. S: green, makes its own food. T: fur, eats plants. Take ecological role as producer, consumer or decomposer.
(i) Group them by ecological role.
(ii) Group them by the feature 'feathers present or absent'.
(iii) Which two organisms are together under both groupings?
(iv) Which two are together by ecological role but apart by feathers?
(v) What does this show about choosing criteria?
questions.a: (i) Producer S; consumers P, Q, T; decomposer R. (ii) Feathers: P, Q; no feathers: R, S, T. (iii) P and Q. (iv) P and T (or Q and T). (v) The grouping changes with the criterion, so scientists use several criteria together.
s: Ecological role: S producer; P, Q, T consumers; R decomposer
Feathers: P and Q; the rest without
P and Q together in both
P and T (or Q and T) together as consumers but apart by feathers
Groups depend on the criterion; several criteria are used

questions.q:
About 300 of India's roughly 1,300 bird species are recorded in Pakke Tiger Reserve. Four hornbill species there nest only in large, old trees and eat specific fruits.
(i) What percentage of India's bird species is recorded in Pakke?
(ii) How many of India's bird species are not recorded there?
(iii) Name one benefit of classification that lets scientists keep track of so many species.
(iv) How does telling the four hornbills apart help scientists?
(v) The forest office wants to fell some large old trees for timber revenue. Give a reasoned view.
questions.a: (i) about 23% (ii) about 1,000 (iii) it makes study organised and systematic (iv) it shows how each species is linked to particular trees and parts of the forest (v) a reasoned view such as not felling the large old trees because the hornbills depend on them for nesting and fruit.
s: Organised, systematic study (or another correct benefit)
Distinguishing species shows distribution and links with plants
A reasoned view that uses the hornbills' dependence on old trees

questions.q:
Kiran finds an organism in a pond. It has many cells, each with a membrane-bound nucleus and a cell wall; it is green and makes its own food; it lives only in water.
(a) Name three criteria from the chapter's list that Kiran's observations use.
(b) Cyanobacteria also make their own food. Why would grouping by mode of nutrition alone put the two together wrongly?
(c) Which observation separates the two?
(d) Should Kiran rely on one criterion or several? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Cell structure, mode of nutrition, level of organisation (and habitat/external features). (b) Both are autotrophic, but one is eukaryotic and the other prokaryotic. (c) The membrane-bound nucleus. (d) Several, because one criterion can group unlike organisms together.
s: Three criteria: cell structure, mode of nutrition, multicellular organisation
Both autotrophic, so nutrition alone cannot separate them
Membrane-bound nucleus (eukaryote) vs none (prokaryote)
Use several criteria, with a reason

questions.q:
A bird club surveys 20 forest sites with large old fruit trees and 20 sites without them. The Great Hornbill is seen at 18 of the sites with large old trees and at 1 of the sites without.
(a) Find the percentage of each type of site where it was seen.
(b) What does the difference suggest about the bird's needs?
(c) Which benefit of classification made it possible to study this species separately from the other three hornbills?
(d) A panchayat can protect only one of two forest patches: one with large old trees, one cleared for plantation. Which should it protect and why?
questions.a: (a) 90% and 5% (b) It depends on large old trees for nesting and fruit (c) Identifying and naming the species (d) The patch with large old trees, as the data shows the species depends on them; a cleared patch offers little for the hornbills.
s: Dependence on large old trees (nesting and fruit)
Classification lets scientists identify and distinguish each hornbill species
A decision supported by the 90% vs 5% data

questions.q: A student places Paramecium in Linnaeus's two kingdom system. It moves from place to place and depends on others for food, which suits Animalia, yet she is uneasy. What is the source of her unease?
questions.a: It is unicellular, whereas the animals and plants of the system are multicellular. The chapter says Amoeba and Paramecium move like animals and are heterotrophic but are unicellular, while plants and animals are multicellular; this confusion led to a third kingdom.
o: It is unicellular, whereas the animals and plants of the system are multicellular
It makes its own food by photosynthesis like the members of Plantae
It has no cell structure at all, so no kingdom can include it
It lacks a nucleus in the way that bacteria lack one

questions.q: With a better microscope, a scientist in the 1930s compares an amoeba with a bacterium. Both are single-celled, yet she moves the bacterium to a new kingdom. What did she observe?
questions.a: The amoeba has a true, membrane-bound nucleus, but the bacterium does not. Improved microscopes showed that amoeba has a membrane-bound nucleus and bacteria do not, so bacteria were placed in the separate kingdom Monera.
o: The amoeba has a true, membrane-bound nucleus, but the bacterium does not
The bacterium makes food by photosynthesis, but the amoeba never does
The bacterium has many cells, while the amoeba has only one
The bacterium moves with tentacles, but the amoeba stays fixed

questions.q: A researcher in 1969 notes that a mushroom does not move like a plant and cannot make its own food, but absorbs nutrients from decaying matter. What did this finding lead to?
questions.a: A separate kingdom, Fungi, since the mushroom fitted neither Plantae nor Animalia well. Fungi are heterotrophic and absorb nutrients but do not move like plants; this made Whittaker (1969) place them in their own kingdom.
o: A separate kingdom, Fungi, since the mushroom fitted neither Plantae nor Animalia well
Its transfer to Monera, because it absorbs food from outside
Its transfer to Animalia, because it cannot make its own food
Its transfer to Protista, because it has a nucleus

questions.q: A student uses Aristotle's habitat idea (land, water, air) and puts a butterfly, an eagle and a bat in the same 'air' group. What limitation of such a system does this show?
questions.a: Grouping by habitat and easily seen outer features can put very different animals together. The chapter says Aristotle's system relied mainly on easily observable external characteristics and habitat, which is its limitation.
o: Grouping by habitat and easily seen outer features can put very different animals together
The system had far too many groups to remember
The system ignored where animals live
The system could be used only for plants

questions.q:
Statement 1: The two kingdom system (Linnaeus, 1758) divided living things into Plantae and Animalia.
Statement 2: The three kingdom system (Haeckel, 1866) added Protista for unicellular microscopic organisms.
Statement 3: Copeland (1938) gave fungi a kingdom of their own.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 only. Statement 3 is false because fungi were given their own kingdom by Whittaker in 1969; Copeland's addition was Monera.
o: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statement 2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Aristotle's habitat-based grouping is still the main system scientists use today.
Reason (R): Classification systems have changed as new tools, such as better microscopes, increased knowledge.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. A is false because the five kingdom system and others replaced it; R is true as the chapter shows each change followed new knowledge.
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q: Counting from Linnaeus's two kingdom system (1758) to Whittaker's five kingdom system (1969), the revision took ___ years.

Match each scientist in List I with the change made to classification in List II.
1. Aristotle
2. Haeckel
3. Copeland
4. Whittaker
a. Added Protista for unicellular microscopic organisms
b. Gave fungi their own kingdom
c. Grouped animals by habitat, as land, water and air
d. Placed bacteria in a separate kingdom, Monera
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-d, 4-b. Aristotle grouped by habitat; Haeckel added Protista; Copeland created Monera; Whittaker created Fungi.

questions.q: True or False? Once microscopes improved, scientists kept amoeba and bacteria together in Protista because both are single-celled. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The improved microscopes showed that an amoeba has a true, membrane-bound nucleus but bacteria do not, so bacteria were moved to a separate kingdom, Monera.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: amoeba has a membrane-bound nucleus, bacteria do not, so bacteria went into Monera

questions.q:
(a) Who added the third kingdom, Protista, and in which year?
(b) Which kind of organisms made the third kingdom necessary?
questions.a: (a) Ernst Haeckel, 1866. (b) Unicellular microscopic organisms such as Amoeba and Paramecium that did not fit plants or animals.
s: Part (a): Haeckel, 1866
Part (b): unicellular microscopic organisms such as Amoeba and Paramecium

questions.q:
(a) In the two kingdom system, state one feature that separated Plantae from Animalia.
(b) Name one organism that this feature could not place satisfactorily and say why.
questions.a: (a) Plantae do not move and make their own food; Animalia move and depend on others for food. (b) Amoeba (or Paramecium or bacteria): it moves like an animal but is unicellular.
s: Part (a): movement and mode of getting food
Part (b): a named organism with the reason, e.g. Amoeba is unicellular

questions.q: Give the observation about mushrooms that led to the fifth kingdom, and say why it did not fit the earlier kingdoms.
questions.a: Mushrooms do not move like plants and are heterotrophic, absorbing nutrients from dead and decaying matter; so they fitted neither Plantae nor Animalia.
s: Observation: heterotrophic, absorbing nutrients, not moving like plants
Reason: fitted neither Plantae nor the animal way of life, so Fungi was created

questions.q: Compare the basis of classification used in the Rigveda and the Brihat Samhita with that of Aristotle.
questions.a: Both used habitat; the Indian texts also used behaviour patterns and ecological roles, whereas Aristotle added external appearance.
s: Common basis: habitat (land, water, air)
Difference: Indian texts add behaviour and ecological roles; Aristotle adds external appearance

questions.q: Meena says, 'Better microscopes alone are responsible for every change in the classification systems.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Partly right. Microscopes showed that bacteria lack a true nucleus, leading to Monera; but fungi were separated by noticing their mode of nutrition, and Protista arose from the confusion about unicellular organisms.
s: Verdict: only partly right
Microscopes explain the creation of Monera
Other changes came from nutrition and the placement problem, not microscopes alone

questions.q: Show that a system that groups animals only by habitat cannot reflect how different a sponge, a jellyfish and a fish are.
questions.a: All three live in water, so habitat puts them in one group; yet they differ greatly in body organisation: sponges have cellular-level organisation, jellyfish tissue-level, and fish have a backbone.
s: All three would fall in the 'water' group
Their body organisation differs: cellular, tissue-level, backbone
So habitat alone hides major differences

questions.q: Describe in three steps how the five kingdom system arose from the two kingdom system.
questions.a: Protista was added for unicellular organisms (1866); bacteria moved to Monera when found to lack a true nucleus (1938); fungi were given their own kingdom for their absorptive nutrition (1969).
s: Protista added for unicellular microscopic organisms
Monera created for organisms lacking a true nucleus
Fungi created for heterotrophs that absorb nutrients

questions.q:
The dated revisions are: two kingdoms in 1758, three in 1866, four in 1938 and five in 1969.
(i) Find the gap in years between each pair of successive revisions.
(ii) Which gap is the shortest?
(iii) Find the total time from the first to the last.
(iv) Name the kingdom added in the shortest gap and the reason.
(v) What does a shrinking gap suggest about the pace of new knowledge?
questions.a: (i) 108, 72 and 31 years (ii) 31 years, 1938 to 1969 (iii) 211 years (iv) Fungi, since they are heterotrophic and absorb nutrients (v) New tools and knowledge arrived faster, so revisions came sooner.
s: Shortest: 31 years
Total 1969 - 1758 = 211 years
Fungi, with the mode-of-nutrition reason
Faster new knowledge, with a reason

questions.q:
Five organisms are: a rose plant, a cow, Amoeba, a bacterium and a mushroom.
(i) In the two kingdom system, which two are easy to place and where?
(ii) Which organism's placement became easier when Protista was added?
(iii) In the four kingdom system, where does the bacterium go?
(iv) Which of the five still has no proper kingdom in the four kingdom system?
(v) Where does it go in the five kingdom system and why?
questions.a: (i) Rose in Plantae, cow in Animalia (ii) Amoeba in Protista (iii) Monera (iv) Mushroom (v) Fungi, because it is heterotrophic and absorbs nutrients.
s: Rose in Plantae, cow in Animalia
Amoeba in Protista
Bacterium in Monera
Mushroom has no fit before five kingdoms
Fungi, with the absorptive nutrition reason

questions.q:
A science club draws a timeline: 1758 two kingdoms, 1866 three, 1938 four, 1969 five. The principal asks whether the school should keep the older systems in the lab chart.
(a) Find the number of years between the two kingdom and four kingdom systems.
(b) State what each of the three later systems added.
(c) Which improvement in tools explains the second change?
(d) Give one argument for and one against keeping the older systems on the chart, then decide.
questions.a: (a) 180 years (b) Protista, Monera, Fungi (c) Better microscopes (d) For: shows how knowledge grew; against: may confuse a beginner; a reasoned decision such as keeping them on a timeline, with the five kingdom system as the working one.
s: Protista, Monera, Fungi in order
Improved microscopes (true nucleus in amoeba, none in bacteria)
One reason each side and a reasoned decision

questions.q:
A forest officer lists four animals. A: lives on land, hunts at night, eats other animals. B: lives on land, active by day, eats plants. C: lives in water, eats algae. D: flies, active by day, eats insects. The Rigveda and the Brihat Samhita classified animals on habitat (terrestrial, aquatic, aerial), behaviour and ecological role.
(a) Group A to D by habitat alone as Aristotle did.
(b) Which pair is together by habitat but separated by behaviour and role?
(c) Name one point the Indian texts add to habitat.
(d) The officer must pick a system to plan night patrols. Which is more useful and why?
questions.a: (a) Land: A, B; water: C; air: D (b) A and B (c) Behaviour patterns or ecological roles (d) The Indian system, because behaviour (hunts at night) is what the patrol needs; habitat alone would mix A with B.
s: Land A and B; water C; air D
A and B: same habitat, different behaviour and role
Behaviour patterns or ecological roles
Choice of the richer system, justified by the night-hunting behaviour

questions.q: Three unknown organisms are examined. X: unicellular, no membrane-bound nucleus, has a cell wall. Y: unicellular, true nucleus, no cell wall, swims using cilia. Z: multicellular, true nucleus, chitin cell wall, no chlorophyll. Which option names their kingdoms in this order?
questions.a: Monera, Protista, Fungi. No true nucleus and unicellular means Monera; a unicellular eukaryote without a cell wall is Protista; a multicellular eukaryote with a chitin wall that cannot make food is Fungi.
o: Monera, Protista, Fungi
Protista, Monera, Fungi
Monera, Fungi, Protista
Fungi, Protista, Monera

questions.q: Ria argues, 'Yeast is a single cell with a true nucleus, so it must go in Protista with Amoeba.' Which reply is correct according to the chapter?
questions.a: Yeast has a cell wall made of chitin, a feature of fungi, so it is placed in Fungi. Yeast is unicellular but its chitin cell wall places it under fungi; Protista has either no cell wall or one of cellulose.
o: Yeast has a cell wall made of chitin, a feature of fungi, so it is placed in Fungi
Yeast has no true nucleus, so it belongs to Monera
Yeast is multicellular, so Protista does not suit it
Yeast makes its own food, so it is classed as a plant

questions.q: A village sets up a biogas plant that runs on cattle dung. Which organisms are responsible for producing biogas from the dung of these animals?
questions.a: Bacteria that live in the gut of ruminants. The chapter states that bacteria (Kingdom Monera) found in the gut of ruminants are responsible for biogas production from their dung.
o: Bacteria that live in the gut of ruminants
Mushrooms that grow on the dung heap
Amoeba swimming in the dung slurry
Spirogyra growing in the water tank

questions.q: Oil and pesticide wastes are polluting a village pond. Which group does the chapter mention as able to break down such pollutants?
questions.a: Some bacteria. The chapter says some bacteria break down pollutants like oil, pesticides and sewage.
o: Some bacteria
All members of Protista, because they swim in water
Mushrooms, because they reproduce by spores
Cyanobacteria alone, because they are autotrophs

questions.q: A single-celled organism with flagella and a true nucleus makes its own food in sunlight. A student says it must be a plant. What is the best classification?
questions.a: Protista, since this kingdom includes both autotrophic and heterotrophic members. Plantae are multicellular; Protista are unicellular eukaryotes and include autotrophic members.
o: Protista, since this kingdom includes both autotrophic and heterotrophic members
Plantae, since anything that makes its own food is a plant
Monera, since all single-celled organisms belong there
Fungi, since single-celled eukaryotes are always fungi

questions.q:
Statement 1: Protista includes only autotrophic organisms.
Statement 2: Yeast is unicellular and still belongs to Kingdom Fungi.
Statement 3: Fungi cannot make their own food and reproduce only sexually.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 only. Statement 1 is false because Protista has autotrophic and heterotrophic members; statement 3 is false because fungi reproduce both sexually and asexually.
o: Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
All three statements
Statement 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Yeast is placed in Kingdom Fungi even though it is unicellular.
Reason (R): Fungi absorb nutrients through a network of fine filaments called mycelium.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both statements are true, but yeast is placed under fungi because its cell wall is made of chitin, not because of its mycelium.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A mushroom grower finishes one batch every 45 days, the longest life cycle the chapter gives. In 360 days he can complete at most ___ batches.

(a) Name any two groups of organisms in Kingdom Monera.
(b) Name one kind of place where they live that most other organisms cannot survive in.
questions.a: (a) Any two of bacteria, archaea, cyanobacteria. (b) Hot springs or other extreme environments.
s: Part (a): two of bacteria, archaea, cyanobacteria
Part (b): hot springs or other extreme environments

questions.q:
A fungus is found growing on a fallen log.
(a) Through which structure does it take in food?
(b) What ecological role does this feeding give it?
questions.a: (a) The mycelium, a network of fine filaments, absorbs nutrients from the dead matter. (b) Decomposer (saprophyte).
s: Part (a): mycelium of fine filaments absorbing nutrients
Part (b): decomposer

questions.q: Differentiate Kingdom Protista from Kingdom Monera on two criteria.
questions.a: Protista are unicellular eukaryotes with a true nucleus, with or without a cellulose cell wall; Monera are unicellular prokaryotes without a membrane-bound nucleus.
s: Cell type: eukaryote (Protista) vs prokaryote (Monera)
Cell wall or other contrast, e.g. Protista with none or cellulose

questions.q: Who is known as the Father of Modern Biogas? State what he set up in 1957 and which kingdom's organisms make biogas.
questions.a: Ram Bux Singh set up India's first scientifically designed biogas plant at Ramnagar, Sitapur, Uttar Pradesh; biogas is produced by bacteria (Monera).
s: Ram Bux Singh and his plant at Ramnagar, Sitapur, in 1957
Biogas is made by bacteria, which belong to Monera

questions.q: Why are stromatolites important, and where have they been found in India?
questions.a: They hold fossils of ancient cyanobacteria and give some of the earliest evidence of life on Earth; they were found in Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh.
s: Fossils of ancient cyanobacteria, earliest evidence of life
Found in Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh

questions.q: Imran says, 'All fungi are multicellular, so yeast cannot be a fungus.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. Fungi are mostly, not always, multicellular; yeast is unicellular but has a chitin cell wall like other fungi, so it is a fungus.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Fungi are mostly multicellular, not all
Yeast has a chitin cell wall, so it belongs to Fungi

questions.q: Write three yes/no questions in order that would sort an unknown microscopic organism into Monera, Protista or Fungi.
questions.a: E.g. Does it have a membrane-bound nucleus? No: Monera. If yes, is its cell wall of chitin? Yes: Fungi. If no wall or a cellulose wall: Protista.
s: A first question on the nucleus separating Monera
A question on cell wall (chitin) separating Fungi
Protista as the remaining result, with a consistent order

questions.q: Explain how fungi and bacteria together help keep forest soil fertile.
questions.a: Fungi feed on fallen leaves and dead organisms, breaking complex organic matter into simpler substances that become minerals in the soil; bacteria also decompose and turn waste into manure; both recycle nutrients.
s: Fungi decompose dead matter into simpler substances
Bacteria convert waste and leaves into manure
Result: minerals return to soil, nutrients recycle

questions.q:
A self-help group runs mushroom beds. Each batch takes 40 days, yields 90 kg and costs Rs 4,200 to prepare; mushrooms sell at Rs 120 per kg. The room is used continuously for 365 days.
(i) Find the whole number of batches possible.
(ii) Find the total yield.
(iii) Find the income.
(iv) Find the profit after preparation costs.
(v) Name two features of mushroom farming that the chapter gives as reasons it suits livelihoods.
questions.a: (i) 9 batches (ii) 810 kg (iii) Rs 97,200 (iv) Rs 59,400 (v) Minimal space and low investment (also a fast life cycle).
s: 365/40 = 9 whole batches
Minimal space, low investment (or fast life cycle)

questions.q:
Five organisms are observed. U: unicellular, no true nucleus, cell wall, lives in a hot spring. V: unicellular, true nucleus, no cell wall, swims using cilia. W: multicellular, true nucleus, chitin wall, absorbs food from dead leaves. X: unicellular, true nucleus, chitin wall. Y: unicellular, no true nucleus, makes food using sunlight.
(i) Name the kingdoms of U and V.
(ii) Name the kingdom of W and give a reason.
(iii) Name the kingdom of X and say why it is not Protista.
(iv) Name the kingdom of Y.
(v) Which of the five are prokaryotes?
questions.a: (i) U Monera, V Protista (ii) W Fungi: chitin wall, absorbs nutrients (iii) X Fungi, because its wall is chitin (iv) Y Monera (a cyanobacterium) (v) U and Y
s: U in Monera and V in Protista
W in Fungi with the chitin/absorption reason
X in Fungi because of the chitin wall
Y in Monera (no true nucleus)
Prokaryotes: U and Y

questions.q:
A village biogas plant is fed with dung from 40 cattle. Assume each animal gives 10 kg of dung a day, each kg of dung gives 0.04 cubic metres of biogas, and a household needs 1.5 cubic metres a day for cooking.
(a) Find the dung available in a day.
(b) Find the biogas produced in a day.
(c) How many households can cook with it, and which group of organisms makes the gas?
(d) The panchayat can spend its funds on the plant or on LPG cylinders for these households. Give one point for and one against building the plant, and decide.
questions.a: (a) 400 kg (b) 16 cubic metres (c) 10 households, using bacteria from ruminant guts (d) For: renewable, uses waste; against: initial cost and upkeep; a reasoned decision.
s: 400 x 0.04 = 16 cubic metres
16/1.5 gives 10 whole households; bacteria of Kingdom Monera
One point each side and a reasoned decision

questions.q:
A class studies a drop of hay-infusion water and counts 100 single-celled organisms with a true nucleus: 40 Paramecium, 15 Amoeba, 25 Euglena and 20 Chlamydomonas. The teacher says Euglena and Chlamydomonas make food using light, while the others feed on other organisms.
(a) What percentage of the organisms make food using light?
(b) Give the kingdom of all four and the two criteria that place them there.
(c) State one role in aquatic food chains for each of the two feeding groups.
(d) A farmer wants more food for small animals in her fish pond. Should she encourage the food-making or the feeding group? Justify.
questions.a: (a) 45% (b) Protista; unicellular and eukaryotic (true nucleus) (c) food-makers produce oxygen and food; feeders act as food for small animals or decomposers (d) A reasoned choice, e.g. encourage food-makers as they form the base of the food chain and add oxygen.
s: Protista: unicellular and eukaryotic
A role for each group in aquatic food chains
A justified choice using food chain roles

questions.q: On a damp school wall in the monsoon, Arun finds a green mat with root-like threads and tiny leaf-like parts. A hand lens shows no vascular tissue. By April the mat is dry and brown. Which class is it, and why does it fail in dry weather?
questions.a: Bryophyta; it needs water to reproduce and has no vascular tissue to carry water. Rhizoids, simple leaf-like parts and dependence on moisture mark bryophytes; they lack vascular tissue and need water for reproduction.
o: Bryophyta; it needs water to reproduce and has no vascular tissue to carry water
Pteridophyta; its roots are too short to reach water deep underground
Gymnosperm; its seeds are exposed on cones and dry out
Thallophyta; it has no body at all and cannot store water

questions.q: A fern and a pine both have xylem and phloem. Why can the pine reproduce on a dry hillside where the fern cannot?
questions.a: Fertilisation in the pine does not need water, and it produces seeds. Pteridophytes need aquatic conditions for reproduction and produce no seeds; gymnosperms do not need water for fertilisation and form seeds.
o: Fertilisation in the pine does not need water, and it produces seeds
The fern has no true roots, stems or leaves
The pine has flowers that draw water from the air
The pine has no vascular tissue and so loses less water

questions.q: Villagers say lichens on trunks near their orchard show that the air is clean. A visitor notices none on trunks beside a busy highway. What does this most likely indicate?
questions.a: The air beside the highway may be polluted, since lichens are sensitive indicators of air quality. The chapter calls lichens natural bioindicators: they change colour with air pollutants and are recognised as signs of a pollution-free environment.
o: The air beside the highway may be polluted, since lichens are sensitive indicators of air quality
Lichens grow only on stones and never on tree trunks
Highway trees are angiosperms, which lichens always avoid
The fungus in the lichen thrives best in polluted air

questions.q: A gulmohar tree and a pine tree both bear seeds. Which feature gives the gulmohar the better chance of spreading its seeds to new places?
questions.a: Fruits that enclose seeds and help to disperse them. Angiosperms bear flowers and fruits; fruits help spread seeds, whereas gymnosperm seeds are exposed on cones.
o: Fruits that enclose seeds and help to disperse them
Needle-like leaves that reduce water loss
Seeds exposed on cones
Rhizoids that spread across the ground

questions.q:
Statement 1: A lichen is a partnership of an autotrophic alga and a heterotrophic fungus.
Statement 2: The seeds of gymnosperms are enclosed within fruits.
Statement 3: Bryophytes have true roots, stems and leaves.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only. Statements 2 and 3 are false: gymnosperm seeds are exposed on cones, and bryophytes only have root-like rhizoids and simple structures.
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Angiosperms are the most diverse group of plants on Earth.
Reason (R): Their flowers attract pollinators and their fruits help spread seeds, so they can occupy a wide range of environments.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. R states the features by which angiosperms spread into varied environments, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: In a cross section of a fern stem, the tissue that carries food to all parts of the plant is the ___.
questions.a: phloem

questions.q:
Match each plant class in List I with its description in List II.
1. Thallophyta
2. Bryophyta
3. Pteridophyta
4. Gymnosperm
a. Seeds exposed on cones; fertilisation does not need water
b. True roots, stems and leaves with xylem and phloem, but no seeds
c. Undifferentiated thallus that exchanges gases and water directly with the surroundings
d. Rhizoids and simple leaf-like parts; needs water to reproduce; no vascular tissue
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-b, 4-a. Thallophyta have an undifferentiated thallus; bryophytes rhizoids and dependence on water; pteridophytes vascular tissue without seeds; gymnosperms exposed seeds on cones.

questions.q: True or False? Bryophytes are said to possess true roots because they have root-like structures. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Their root-like structures are rhizoids; bryophytes have no true roots, stems or leaves, which first appear in pteridophytes.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: rhizoids are only root-like; true roots, stems and leaves first appear in pteridophytes

questions.q:
(a) Name the two tissues in a fern stem and say what each carries.
(b) Even with these tissues, why does a fern still need aquatic conditions?
questions.a: (a) Xylem carries water and phloem carries food. (b) Its reproduction needs water; it also produces no seeds.
s: Part (a): xylem carries water, phloem carries food
Part (b): reproduction requires aquatic conditions

questions.q:
(a) To which plant class does a pine belong?
(b) State two features that help the pine survive in cold, dry regions.
questions.a: (a) Gymnosperm. (b) Any two of: needle-like or scale-like leaves reduce water loss; fertilisation needs no water; seeds protect the embryo and hold stored food.
s: Part (a): Gymnosperm
Part (b): two correct survival features

questions.q: Name the two partners of a lichen and explain why a lichen can be used to judge air quality.
questions.a: A lichen is an autotrophic alga with a heterotrophic fungus; it changes colour with air pollutants, so its colour shows how much pollutant is in the air.
s: Partners: an alga and a fungus
Colour changes with air pollutants, so it is a bioindicator

questions.q: Explain why angiosperms are the most diverse plant group, naming the role of flowers and of fruits.
questions.a: Flowers attract pollinators and so make reproduction more efficient; fruits help spread seeds to new locations; together they let angiosperms live in a wide range of environments.
s: Flowers attract pollinators and increase reproduction
Fruits spread seeds to new locations, widening the range

questions.q: Reena says, 'Hortus Malabaricus was written by a European alone and shows that Indian traditional knowledge had no place in botany.' Check her claim.
questions.a: No. It was compiled in the 17th century by Hendrik van Rheede with the help of Itty Achudan, an Indian herbalist, botanist and physician, and other local experts, and shows traditional knowledge and science working together.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
It was compiled with Itty Achudan and other local experts
It describes hundreds of species and uses, showing traditional knowledge and science together

questions.q: Write three clues that together point to Pteridophyta and to no other plant class.
questions.a: E.g. it has true roots, stems and leaves; it has xylem and phloem; it still needs water to reproduce and bears no seeds.
s: Clue naming true roots, stems and leaves
Clue naming vascular tissue
Clue naming dependence on water and absence of seeds

questions.q: Compare bryophytes and pteridophytes on three points: body parts, transport tissue and reproduction.
questions.a: Bryophytes have rhizoids and simple structures; pteridophytes have true roots, stems and leaves. Bryophytes lack vascular tissue; pteridophytes have xylem and phloem. Both need water for reproduction and neither makes seeds.
s: Body parts compared
Transport tissue compared
Reproduction: both need water, neither has seeds

questions.q:
Five plants are described. A: thallus body, lives in a pond. B: needle-like leaves, seeds on cones. C: rhizoids, grows as green mats on damp soil. D: true roots, stems and leaves, xylem and phloem, no seeds. E: flowers and fruits.
(i) Name the class of A and of B.
(ii) Name the class of C and of D.
(iii) Name the class of E.
(iv) Arrange A to E from least to most adapted to life on land.
(v) Of B, C and D, which does not need water for fertilisation?
questions.a: (i) A Thallophyta, B Gymnosperm (ii) C Bryophyta, D Pteridophyta (iii) E Angiosperm (iv) A, C, D, B, E (v) B
s: A Thallophyta, B Gymnosperm
C Bryophyta, D Pteridophyta
E Angiosperm
Order A, C, D, B, E
B (gymnosperm) needs no water for fertilisation; C and D do

questions.q:
A school garden survey records 50 plants: 8 mosses, 6 ferns, 4 pines, 28 flowering plants and 4 pond algae.
(i) What percentage are angiosperms?
(ii) What percentage need water for reproduction while living on land (mosses and ferns)?
(iii) What percentage produce seeds?
(iv) Name the recorded class that has vascular tissue but no seeds.
(v) What does the answer to (iii) suggest about the success of seeds on land?
questions.a: (i) 56% (ii) 28% (iii) 64% (iv) Pteridophyta (ferns) (v) Seed-bearing plants are the majority, which fits seeds helping plants live on land.
s: Pteridophyta
A reasoned link between seeds and success on land

questions.q:
Lichen cover on tree trunks is measured at three sites of a hill town: Site A (forest edge) 80% of trunks, Site B (town road) 35%, Site C (highway junction) 5%. About 20,000 people pass Site B daily and 3,000 pass Site C.
(a) How many percentage points lower is cover at B and at C than at A?
(b) What does the pattern suggest about the air at the three sites, and why?
(c) Name the two partners in a lichen and the feature that makes it an indicator.
(d) Funds allow pollution control at only one site now. Choose one, with a reason that weighs the data.
questions.a: (a) 45 and 75 percentage points (b) Air is cleanest at A and worst at C, since lichens are sensitive to air pollutants (c) alga and fungus; colour change with pollutants (d) A reasoned choice: C has the worst air, B affects far more people.
s: Pollution lowest at A, highest at C, with the lichen link
Alga and fungus; colour change with pollutants
A choice weighing pollution level against people exposed

questions.q:
For a science fair, four exhibits are set up: Spirogyra in a tank, moss on a damp tray, a fern in a pot and a young pine in a pot. A power cut stops the water supply for three days.
(a) Which exhibits need aquatic conditions to reproduce?
(b) Which exhibits have no xylem and phloem?
(c) Which exhibit is adapted to dry conditions and why?
(d) Rank the exhibits from most to least likely to cope with the three days without water. Justify the order.
questions.a: (a) Moss and fern (Spirogyra is aquatic) (b) Spirogyra and moss (c) Pine, with needle-like leaves that reduce water loss (d) Pine, fern, moss, Spirogyra, with a reason based on dependence on water.
s: Moss and fern need water for reproduction
Spirogyra and moss lack vascular tissue
Pine: leaves reduce water loss, fertilisation needs no water
A ranking with reasons about water dependence

questions.q: A doctor examines a worm taken from a child's gut. It is flattened, has two similar sides, a single opening for food and waste, and hooks and suckers at one end. Which phylum does it belong to, and what clinches it?
questions.a: Platyhelminthes, since it is flat, bilaterally symmetrical and has one opening. Flatworms show bilateral symmetry, have one opening, and parasitic forms use hooks and suckers; roundworms have two openings.
o: Platyhelminthes, since it is flat, bilaterally symmetrical and has one opening
Nematoda, since it has hooks and suckers and a digestive system
Annelida, since it lives in a host and has muscles and a nerve cord
Cnidaria, since it has one opening for food and waste

questions.q: An earthworm and a beetle both have segmented bodies, yet the beetle survives on dry, exposed ground that would kill the earthworm. What best explains the beetle's advantage?
questions.a: Its hard external skeleton protects it, reduces water loss and supports its muscles. The chapter says an arthropod's hard exoskeleton provides protection, reduces water loss and supports powerful muscles.
o: Its hard external skeleton protects it, reduces water loss and supports its muscles
It has a notochord that keeps its body from drying
It has more segments than the earthworm
It has no organ-system level of organisation

questions.q: A starfish has a hard internal skeleton of calcium carbonate. A student says it must therefore be a vertebrate. What is the correct placement?
questions.a: Invertebrate, in Echinodermata, because it lacks a notochord despite its internal skeleton. Animals are divided first by the notochord; echinoderms have no notochord, so they are non-chordata.
o: Invertebrate, in Echinodermata, because it lacks a notochord despite its internal skeleton
Vertebrate, because any internal skeleton means a backbone
Protochordate, because internal support appears in protochordates
Arthropoda, because it has a hard skeleton

questions.q: A small marine animal has a notochord during part of its life but never develops a backbone. Where does it belong?
questions.a: Protochordata, within Chordata. Protochordates (like Amphioxus) possess a notochord at least once in their life; vertebrates have a vertebral column.
o: Protochordata, within Chordata
Vertebrata, because a notochord is a backbone
Non-chordata, because it has no vertebral column
Echinodermata, because it has internal support

questions.q: Why does a forest rich in animal species lower the risk of Kyasanur Forest Disease (monkey fever) in the Western Ghats, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Many of the animals are hosts in which the virus cannot replicate, acting as a biological barrier. The chapter says forest diversity acts as a biological barrier because many animals are hosts where the virus cannot replicate.
o: Many of the animals are hosts in which the virus cannot replicate, acting as a biological barrier
The animals eat all the ticks, so none is left
The virus replicates faster when there are more hosts
Forest soil kills the virus before it reaches animals

questions.q:
Statement 1: Sponges have tissues but no organs.
Statement 2: Vertebrates are divided into five groups on the basis of a hard external skeleton.
Statement 3: Parasitic flatworms use hooks and suckers to attach to host tissues.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 3 only. Statement 1 is false because sponges have cellular-level organisation with no tissues; statement 2 is false because the groups are based on habitat use, body covering and reproduction.
o: Statement 3 only
Statement 2 only
Statement 1 only
All three statements

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Arthropods can survive in dry and exposed environments.
Reason (R): Arthropods have segmented bodies.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both are true, but survival in dry places is explained by the hard exoskeleton that reduces water loss, not by segmentation alone.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:

questions.q: True or False? Echinoderms are classed with the chordates because they have a hard internal skeleton. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.

questions.q: Parasitic worms enter the body through contaminated water and food. Give two habits that reduce the risk.
questions.a: Any two of: wash hands properly and keep personal hygiene, eat properly cooked food, drink boiled or filtered water, good sanitary habits.

Second correct precaution

questions.q: State two functions of the vertebral column, and one benefit it gives the animal's body.
questions.a: It supports the body and protects vital organs such as the brain and spinal cord; it allows a larger body size, efficient movement and complex organ systems.

One benefit such as larger size or efficient movement

questions.q: Sana says, 'When the super cyclone of 1999 hit Orissa, villages with more mangroves had less destruction, so conserving biodiversity can protect people.' Check her claim.

Evidence: villages with more mangroves suffered less in 1999
Conclusion: biodiversity acts as a barrier, so conserving it protects people

questions.q: A parasite found in a host has only one opening for food and waste. Show that it cannot be a nematode, and name the phylum it could belong to.

One opening therefore cannot be a nematode
Platyhelminthes fits: one opening, parasitic forms

questions.q: Choose fish, birds and mammals. For each, name one structural feature and say how it helps survival.
questions.a: Fish: fins and gills for moving and breathing in water. Birds: feathers and hollow bones make flight possible. Mammals: mammary glands improve the survival of the young.

Birds: feathers and hollow bones with the benefit

questions.q:

questions.q:

questions.q:
